q: What is El Niño?
a: El Niño is when the sea surface in the middle and east of the Pacific Ocean gets warmer than normal for several months. It comes every 2 to 7 years and usually lasts about a year. That warm water changes winds and rain around the world, including West Africa.

q: What is La Niña?
a: La Niña is the opposite: the same part of the Pacific gets cooler than normal. When neither is happening, scientists call it "neutral".

q: How do scientists know El Niño is happening?
a: NOAA, the US weather agency, measures Pacific sea temperatures every month. When the Niño index stays more than 0.5 °C above normal, they call it El Niño. The platform shows this index on its Overview tab.

q: How does El Niño affect Liberia?
a: It usually weakens the West African monsoon, so Liberia can get longer dry spells and hotter days. But the Atlantic Ocean near Liberia matters just as much, so El Niño years do not all look the same.

q: Does El Niño always mean less rain?
a: No. In 2023–24, El Niño and a warm Indian Ocean pattern kept rain falling unusually long on Liberia's coast. Floods are still possible in an El Niño year.

q: What do Low, Watch and Warning mean?
a: They are EPA's working levels on the Hazard Map. For floods, Warning means at least 10% of people in that area live in the 1-in-100-year flood zone; Watch means at least 3%. Dryness levels come from FAO's crop stress data. The "How this is calculated" note on each map explains them.

q: What is a "1-in-100-year flood zone"?
a: Land that has a 1% chance of flooding in any year from rivers overflowing. It can flood two years in a row; "100 years" is about the odds, not a timetable.

q: What should I do after a flood?
a: Use only boiled, treated or bottled water for drinking and cooking. Wash hands with soap. Go to a health facility quickly if anyone has bad diarrhoea or vomiting, because floods can spread cholera.
